body_text:
Keynote Address by Deputy Governor Adnan Zaylani Mohamad Zahid
at Beyond Books: Library & Learning Innovation Talk 2026
Kuala Lumpur | 29 October 2026
It is a pleasure to join you today for the inaugural Beyond Books: Library & Learning Innovation Talk 2026, or LIT 2026.
Let me begin by congratulating the Financial Services Library (FSL), together with Asia School of Business (ASB) and INCEIF University, for putting this programme together. The theme Beyond Books poses an interesting and important question. Being an avid book reader, I couldn’t help but eagerly accept this opportunity to share my thoughts on this. I have to admit though, I hardly ever find myself in any library these days but I am certainly happy to be here today.
My own meaningful experiences in libraries was in secondary boarding school and all the way to my university days. At first, and in the 80s, in a rural boarding school in Terengganu, tucked away from the outside world, no TV nor smartphones and internet, the library was a place you could escape from this cocooned existence. Only in the library, can you get the resources and books, to open your minds and travel to distant places, discover unusual things and, my favourite pastime, learn history and civilisations. In my university years, the library was a place of quiet study, and the only place often, that you can get the recommended articles to read, the out-of-print textbooks to refer to.
Many of us of the earlier generations share similar experiences. As students, researchers or professionals, a library has at some point helped us as a place to study, research, find answers or validate ideas. Libraries mattered.
The Changing Landscape
But today, more often than not, some may think libraries are a relic of the past. In this digital age, information and knowledge is at our fingertips, there is no need to clutter ourselves with books, we can go digital. In fact, libraries are hardly visited by working professionals and are mainly frequented rather infrequently by students, researchers and academia.
The digital era has changed the equation. Information has become increasingly abundant and accessible. Vast amounts of knowledge can now be accessed from almost anywhere. There is another inflection point. Artificial intelligence is transforming how information is searched, analysed and even generated.
Given this, what would happen to libraries as we know them?
How do we ensure libraries remain relevant and with a strong purpose?
Allow me to offer my own few reflections on this.
Reflection 1: From Knowledge Repository to Knowledge Hub
First, libraries have, since time immemorial, been repositories of knowledge. Today, knowledge itself is increasingly everywhere and abundant. Making sense of the vast amounts of knowledge, can be challenging. What matters now is the ability to connect people with trusted sources, relevant expertise and meaningful understanding.
Libraries thus have the opportunity to evolve from just knowledge repositories into knowledge hubs. They can help transform information into insight, and insight into action. This is where library professionals become important. Their value lies not only in providing access, but in curating, contextualising and connecting knowledge so users can navigate better in a complex information environment. For a specialised institution such as FSL, this role is especially significant. Its strength lies not in offering the broadest collection, but in providing trusted financial-sector knowledge and helping users derive value from it.
Reflection 2: From Centre of Study to Centre of Innovation
Second, on innovation. Traditionally, libraries have been seen as centres of study, supporting learning and research. That role remains important. But increasingly, libraries also have an opportunity to serve as centres of innovation. In the financial sector, innovation rarely occurs in isolation. It emerges when different perspectives, disciplines and experiences come together.
The same applies to knowledge. Universities generate research. Policymakers provide institutional perspectives. Industry contributes practical experience. Libraries create opportunities for these communities to meet, exchange ideas and generate new thinking.
This principle already is being reflected in initiatives such as the Global Islamic Economist Programme launched by INCEIF University, Bank Negara Malaysia and the Islamic Development Bank. The programme is designed specifically to bridge academic theory with practical policymaking and develop future talent in Islamic economics and finance.
We also see it reflected in the collaboration between FSL, ASB and INCEIF. The value lies not only in bringing institutions together, but in creating new opportunities for learning, experimentation and innovation.
Reflection 3: From Place of Knowledge to Place of Culture
Third, libraries are ultimately about people. Libraries today can bring people together. In this, libraries have the opportunity to evolve from places of knowledge into places of culture. They create spaces that encourage curiosity, dialogue and lifelong learning. They create spaces for diversity, tolerance and respect for each other to thrive.
For students, this means connecting classroom learning with real-world challenges while gaining a better understanding of different communities, perspectives and experiences. For library and knowledge professionals, it means continuously adapting their skills while creating spaces for learning, dialogue and connection.
Even as technology evolves, the importance of culture, values and human connection remains unchanged. In a diverse society such as Malaysia, libraries can be another place that helps foster understanding, respect and a shared sense of community. Ultimately, resilient institutions are built not only on systems and infrastructure, but on people who continue to learn, adapt and grow together.
Before I conclude, I just would like to acknowledge as well as encourage all of us to reflect on the decline of reading as a culture and the view of shallow thinking in the digital age. Indeed, this is the challenge before us and hence why events such as this could be important junctures for us to take stock and reinvigorate the culture.
One final thought. The future of libraries should not be judged by how digital, sophisticated or innovative they become. The more important thing is whether they continue to create value for people and institutions.
Can they help transform information into understanding?
Can they bring together different communities to generate new ideas?
Can they create cultures that encourage learning, innovation and collaboration?
If we can answer these questions positively, libraries will remain important not despite technological change, but because of it. For FSL, ASB and INCEIF, there is an opportunity to think beyond individual institutions and consider what could be achieved collectively.
Together, we can contribute not only to knowledge access, but also to the development of a broader financial-sector knowledge, innovation and a culture hub. I hope LIT 2026 becomes one platform that advances that journey.
Thank you.

Ucapan Timbalan Gabenor Adnan Zaylani Mohamad Zahid
di Majlis Penutup Karnival Celik Kewangan Selangor 2026
dan Bulan Literasi Kewangan 2026
Shah Alam | 25 Oktober 2026
Alhamdulillah, pada petang ini kita tiba di penghujung Karnival Celik Kewangan Selangor, sekali gus melabuhkan tirai Bulan Literasi Kewangan 2026. Sepanjang tiga hari yang lalu, Central i-City bukan sahaja menjadi tempat orang ramai membeli-belah dan meluangkan masa bersama keluarga, malah turut menjadi ruang untuk mereka bertanya, belajar dan mendapatkan panduan berkaitan kewangan. Terima kasih saya ucapkan kepada semua pihak yang telah menjayakan penganjuran karnival ini.
Malam ini, reruai akan dikemas dan karnival ini akan berakhir. Namun, persoalan kewangan rakyat akan terus ada pada hari esok. Bil perlu dibayar, anak-anak perlu disekolahkan dan ibu bapa perlu dijaga. Ada pula yang sedang memikirkan soal pekerjaan, perumahan dan persediaan untuk hari tua.
Justeru, pada petang ini, saya ingin mengajak kita semua memikirkan satu persoalan: Apakah yang akan kita teruskan selepas karnival ini berakhir? Persoalan ini penting kerana bagi kebanyakan keluarga, gaji yang diterima setiap bulan bukan sekadar angka dalam akaun. Di sebalik angka itu terdapat keperluan, harapan dan tanggungjawab. Setiap ringgit perlu diurus dengan pertimbangan yang baik. Dalam erti kata lain, wang ialah satu amanah. Prinsip memelihara harta, atau
hifz al-mal
, mengingatkan kita supaya tidak mensia-siakan sumber yang telah diamanahkan kepada kita.
Namun begitu, mengurus amanah ini bukanlah sesuatu yang sentiasa mudah. Ada yang terpaksa membuat pilihan sukar kerana pendapatan yang terhad. Ada yang kurang memahami pilihan kewangan yang tersedia dan ada juga yang berasa segan untuk bertanya atau mendapatkan bantuan. Oleh sebab itulah pendidikan kewangan bukan sekadar menyampaikan nasihat. Kita perlu mendekati masyarakat dengan memahami keadaan mereka, supaya nasihat yang diberikan benar-benar relevan dan dapat diamalkan.
Inilah semangat yang dibawa oleh Skuad Celik Kewangan sepanjang bulan Oktober. Berdasarkan laporan awal, skuad ini telah mengunjungi 72 lokasi di seluruh negara dan menyantuni lebih 17,000 rakyat Malaysia. Mereka turun ke sekolah, institusi pengajian tinggi, tempat kerja, pasar dan komuniti setempat. Pendekatan secara bersemuka memberikan peluang kepada orang ramai untuk mengemukakan soalan yang mungkin tidak pernah mereka tanyakan sebelum ini.
Berdasarkan pemerhatian di sepanjang Jelajah Bulan Literasi Kewangan 2026, ramai rakyat yang disantuni oleh Skuad Celik Kewangan di seluruh negara menunjukkan minat untuk mendapatkan panduan tentang pengurusan hutang, perlindungan dan persediaan persaraan. Hal ini menunjukkan bahawa rakyat sedia bertanya apabila bantuan hadir dekat dengan mereka. Di karnival ini pula, lebih 30,000 pengunjung berpeluang berinteraksi dengan 44 pempamer melalui pelbagai aktiviti dan sesi penerangan.
Pencapaian ini sememangnya wajar dihargai. Namun, pencapaian sebenar kita bukan hanya diukur melalui jumlah lokasi, pengunjung atau pempamer. Yang lebih penting ialah memastikan pintu yang telah kita buka sepanjang bulan ini tidak tertutup semula selepas bulan Oktober. Saya ingin menitipkan
tiga harapan
kepada semua rakan FEN. Tiga harapan ini juga menjadi jambatan antara pencapaian karnival ini dengan tindakan yang perlu kita teruskan selepas ini.
Pertama
, jadikan pendidikan kewangan satu hubungan yang berterusan, bukan sekadar program dalam kalendar. Seseorang mungkin mendengar penerangan semasa karnival ini, tetapi hanya berdepan dengan keputusan sebenar beberapa bulan kemudian. Pastikan mereka tahu di mana hendak mendapatkan maklumat yang sahih, siapa yang boleh dihubungi dan bagaimana mendapatkan panduan susulan.
Kedua
, bawa pendidikan kewangan ke tempat rakyat menjalani kehidupan seharian; di sekolah, di tempat kerja, di pasar, di kawasan perumahan dan dalam komuniti. Kita tidak boleh mengharapkan semua orang datang ke dewan ceramah atau mencari bahan secara dalam talian. Cara kita mendekati seorang pelajar, peniaga kecil atau pesara mungkin berbeza. Yang penting bukanlah menyeragamkan pendekatan, tetapi memastikan manfaatnya sampai kepada mereka.
Ketiga
, dengar dengan teliti perkara yang ditanyakan oleh masyarakat. Soalan yang berulang kali dikemukakan mungkin menjadi petunjuk bahawa penerangan kita masih belum mencukupi. Persoalan yang jarang didengar pula mungkin datang daripada kelompok yang selama ini kurang diberikan perhatian. Bawalah penemuan ini dalam perancangan bersama di bawah
Strategi Kebangsaan Literasi Kewangan 2026–2030
.
Saya berharap setiap rakan FEN pulang daripada karnival ini dengan satu langkah susulan yang jelas, walaupun kecil. Kerjasama kita sepatutnya dirasai dalam kehidupan masyarakat sepanjang tahun, bukan hanya ketika bulan sambutan. Salah satu bentuk kesinambungan itu dapat kita lihat melalui inisiatif yang akan dilancarkan pada petang ini.
Inisiatif ini mencerminkan harapan kedua yang saya sebut tadi, iaitu memastikan manfaat pendidikan kewangan sampai kepada setiap individu, walaupun pendekatannya berbeza. Bagi sesetengah murid, ini bermakna menyediakan bahan pembelajaran dalam format yang lebih mudah diakses. Sempena majlis ini, sukacita saya melancarkan
Modul Celik Kewangan Versi Braille
, yang dibangunkan oleh Bank Simpanan Nasional (BSN), dengan kerjasama Bahagian Pendidikan Khas, Kementerian Pendidikan Malaysia (KPM).
Sejak 2023, Modul Celik Kewangan BSN-KPM telah membantu pelajar sekolah memahami asas kewangan, daripada mengurus wang dan menabung sehingga mengurus hutang serta memahami perlindungan kewangan. Dengan versi Braille ini, murid ketidakupayaan penglihatan dapat mempelajari asas pengurusan kewangan yang sama bersama rakan-rakan mereka, serta membina keyakinan untuk membuat keputusan kewangan sendiri dalam kehidupan seharian. Melalui kerjasama seperti inilah, pendidikan kewangan dapat menjadi lebih inklusif dan membuka peluang yang sama kepada setiap murid.
Daripada usaha bersama ini, izinkan saya beralih kepada pesanan yang lebih khusus kepada para pengunjung dan seluruh rakyat Malaysia.
Tidak semua perkara berkaitan wang mempunyai jawapan yang sama untuk setiap orang. Keputusan yang baik bergantung pada kemampuan dan keperluan kita sendiri. Sebelum mengambil sebarang komitmen kewangan, luangkan masa untuk membandingkan pilihan, memahami jumlah kos dan memikirkan risiko sekiranya keadaan berubah. Jangan hanya menilai kemampuan untuk membayar komitmen kewangan pada bulan ini; fikirkan juga kemampuan pada bulan-bulan mendatang. Berbincanglah tentang kewangan dengan keluarga, dengan penuh hormat dan tanpa saling menyalahkan. Jika ada perkara yang tidak difahami, bertanyalah. Jika menghadapi kesukaran, dapatkan nasihat lebih awal melalui saluran yang dipercayai, termasuk khidmat nasihat percuma AKPK. Meminta bantuan bukan tanda kegagalan; sebaliknya, tindakan itu menunjukkan bahawa kita mengambil tanggungjawab terhadap masa depan.
Sebelum mengakhiri ucapan, saya ingin merakamkan penghargaan kepada seluruh ahli dan rakan FEN, agensi kerajaan, institusi kewangan, pertubuhan masyarakat, para pempamer, sukarelawan, pihak pengurusan Central i-City serta pasukan penganjur. Terima kasih kerana membawa ilmu kewangan lebih dekat kepada masyarakat dan kerana memastikan usaha ini tidak terhenti setakat penganjuran karnival. Akhir kata, setiap karnival mempunyai pembukaan dan penghujungnya. Namun, amanah untuk membantu rakyat mengurus kewangan dengan lebih yakin tidak berakhir mengikut tarikh di kalendar.
Biarlah ilmu yang dipelajari di sini dibawa pulang, dibincangkan di rumah dan digunakan ketika membuat pilihan dalam kehidupan. Biarlah usaha FEN terus berada dekat dengan rakyat pada waktu dan ketika mereka memerlukannya. Itulah makna yang ingin kita hidupkan melalui tema
“Bijak Wang Dulu, Tenang Bila Perlu”
.
Dengan lafaz Bismillahirrahmanirrahim, saya dengan sukacitanya mengisytiharkan Karnival Celik Kewangan Selangor dan Bulan Literasi Kewangan 2026 ditutup secara rasmi.
Sekian, terima kasih.

Ucapan Perasmian oleh Gabenor Dato' Sri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour
di Karnival Celik Kewangan Selangor 2026
Shah Alam | 24 Oktober 2026
Alhamdulillah, kita dapat bersama-sama meraikan majlis perasmian Karnival Celik Kewangan Selangor 2026. Saya turut mengalu-alukan para pengunjung Central i-City yang hadir bersama keluarga dan rakan-rakan.
Pusat beli-belah ialah tempat yang sesuai untuk kita berbicara tentang kewangan. Di sinilah kita membuat banyak keputusan mengenai wang:
apa yang perlu dibeli;
apa yang boleh ditangguhkan; dan
apa yang harus disimpan untuk masa hadapan.
Keputusan-keputusan ini mungkin kecil. Namun, keputusan ini membentuk kehidupan dan kesejahteraan kewangan kita semua.
Tahun ini menandakan ulang tahun kesepuluh FEN. Sepanjang satu dekad, ahli-ahli FEN, institusi kewangan, agensi kerajaan dan rakan-rakan strategik telah bekerjasama untuk memperluas pendidikan kewangan dan mendekati lebih banyak lapisan masyarakat.
Kita wajar berbangga dengan asas yang telah dibina.
Bagi dekad seterusnya, kita perlu meningkatkan impak agar kemajuan itu membawa perubahan yang lebih bermakna. Yang saya maksudkan ialah keputusan yang lebih baik, perlindungan yang lebih kukuh dan daya tahan yang lebih tinggi.
Untuk memahami perjalanan ini, izinkan saya menggunakan tiga tempoh masa: “Sepuluh saat, sepuluh bulan dan sepuluh tahun.”
Pertama, sepuluh saat.
Dalam dunia digital, sepuluh saat sudah memadai untuk membuat pembayaran atau memindahkan wang. Kemudahan ini banyak manfaatnya.
Namun, kepantasan transaksi turut mengehadkan ruang untuk pertimbangan yang lebih mendalam. Beberapa saat boleh menentukan sama ada simpanan keluarga kekal selamat atau hilang.
Bayangkan seseorang menerima panggilan daripada individu yang menyamar sebagai pegawai bank atau pihak berkuasa. Beliau didesak memindahkan wang segera kononnya untuk mengelakkan akaun disekat.
Pada tahun 2025, kerugian akibat penipuan dalam talian mencecah hampir RM3 bilion dengan Selangor merekodkan jumlah kerugian tertinggi
[1]
menurut laporan Kementerian Dalam Negeri.
Dalam hal ini, Bank Negara Malaysia, institusi kewangan dan agensi penguatkuasaan terus memperkukuh pertahanan, termasuk mempercepat pengesanan dana yang dicuri dan memperketat langkah keselamatan perbankan dalam talian. Namun, sistem yang kukuh sahaja tidak mencukupi. Perlindungan pertama tetap bermula dengan kewaspadaan kita sendiri.
Oleh sebab itu, apabila didesak untuk bertindak segera, berhenti seketika. Semak melalui saluran rasmi sebelum berkongsi maklumat atau memindahkan wang. Institusi kewangan pula perlu memperkukuh kawalan, memperjelas amaran dan bertindak pantas terhadap aktiviti yang mencurigakan.
Perlindungan yang berkesan memerlukan kewaspadaan pengguna dan institusi kewangan bergerak seiring.
Kedua, sepuluh bulan.
Jika sepuluh saat menggambarkan satu keputusan, sepuluh bulan pula menggambarkan satu tabiat. Daya tahan kewangan tidak terbina dalam sehari. Sebaliknya, daya tahan ini dibina melalui amalan yang konsisten, bulan demi bulan. Menyimpan secara berkala, merancang perbelanjaan, mengurus komitmen mengikut kemampuan dan mendapatkan nasihat adalah antara langkah mudah yang boleh diamalkan secara konsisten.
Inisiatif seperti #BijakWangChallenge
[2]
menjadikan pembelajaran kewangan lebih menarik kepada generasi muda. Tahun ini, lebih 3,000 peserta dari seluruh negara telah menyertai cabaran ini. Tahniah kepada semua peserta atas kesediaan melabur masa dalam menimba ilmu yang akan membantu mereka membuat keputusan kewangan yang lebih baik sepanjang hayat mereka.
Dalam kehidupan sebenar, kebijaksanaan bukan sekadar mengetahui jawapan tetapi juga mengenal pasti masa yang sesuai untuk berhenti, bertanya dan mendapatkan nasihat.
Ketiga, sepuluh tahun.
Dalam tempoh sepuluh tahun, seseorang mungkin membina keluarga, membeli rumah atau membuat persediaan untuk persaraan. Pada masa yang sama, mereka juga mungkin berhadapan dengan masalah kesihatan, kemalangan atau kehilangan pendapatan.
Pada saat itulah nilai perlindungan dan daya tahan benar-benar terserlah. Simpanan kecemasan, perlindungan yang sesuai dan akses kepada bantuan boleh menentukan sama ada sesuatu kejutan dapat diurus dengan tenang atau menjadi krisis yang berpanjangan.
Sehubungan dengan itu, pelancaran MediAsas di seluruh negara mulai akhir bulan Januari 2027 merupakan langkah penting untuk memperluas akses kepada perlindungan perubatan asas yang lebih mampu milik dan mampan. Pelan ini akan ditadbir dan diurus melalui kerjasama antara kerajaan dengan industri bagi membantu mengawal kos penjagaan kesihatan secara lebih berkesan.
Namun, perlindungan sebenar bukan sekadar memiliki sesuatu produk tetapi juga memahami perlindungan tersebut, memastikan kesesuaiannya dengan keperluan dan memperoleh bantuan apabila diperlukan.
Keperluan ini berbeza bagi setiap individu, termasuk mereka yang memerlukan pendekatan yang lebih khusus untuk memahami dan mendapatkan perlindungan kewangan. Sehubungan dengan itu, hari ini, saya berbesar hati melancarkan
MyCoverageOKU,
iaitu Laman Mikro Insurans dan Takaful untuk Orang Kurang Upaya. Inisiatif ini merupakan hasil kerjasama Bank Negara Malaysia, FEN serta industri insurans dan takaful.
MyCoverageOKU
menghimpunkan maklumat tentang pilihan perlindungan yang relevan kepada golongan OKU. Laman mikro ini menyediakan satu tempat rujukan untuk mereka, ahli keluarga dan penjaga mereka bagi meneroka produk serta menghubungi penyedia insurans dan takaful yang berkaitan. Kelayakan dan manfaat perlindungan tetap tertakluk pada terma dan syarat masing-masing.
Pendekatan yang berteraskan keperluan pengguna ini perlu menjadi panduan dalam kita merangka perkhidmatan kewangan. Cerapan tingkah laku atau
behavioural insights
membantu kita memahami faktor yang mempengaruhi keputusan pengguna. Dalam hal ini, AI juga berpotensi memudahkan penyampaian maklumat, mengesan aktiviti luar biasa dan memberikan peringatan pada waktu yang tepat.
Namun, teknologi tidak seharusnya menggantikan pertimbangan pengguna. Sebaliknya, teknologi perlu membantu pengguna memahami implikasi setiap pilihan, melindungi data peribadi serta memastikan sokongan tetap tersedia.
Kemajuan teknologi telah menjadikan transaksi semakin mudah dan pantas. Pada masa yang sama, institusi kewangan dan pengguna mempunyai peranan bersama dalam memastikan teknologi dimanfaatkan untuk menyokong keputusan kewangan yang lebih baik.
Bagi dekad seterusnya, usaha kita perlu dinilai melalui hasil yang benar-benar dirasai rakyat:
Adakah mereka membuat keputusan yang lebih baik?
Adakah mereka mempunyai perlindungan yang lebih kukuh?
Adakah mereka lebih bersedia menghadapi perkara yang tidak dijangka?
Sepuluh saat mengingatkan kita supaya berhenti seketika.
Sepuluh bulan mendidik kita untuk membina tabiat.
Sepuluh tahun menuntut persediaan dan perlindungan untuk menghadapi pelbagai kemungkinan.
Jika kita menghubungkan ketiga-tiganya, pendidikan kewangan bukan sahaja menambah pengetahuan. Pendidikan kewangan juga membantu rakyat menjalani kehidupan kewangan yang lebih selamat, yakin dan sejahtera.
Saya merakamkan penghargaan khususnya kepada Kerajaan Negeri Selangor serta ahli-ahli dan rakan strategik FEN, pihak industri dan semua pihak yang telah berganding bahu menjayakan Karnival ini.
Dengan usaha bersama, insya-Allah kita dapat membina masyarakat Malaysia yang lebih terlindung, lebih berdaya tahan dan menikmati kehidupan kewangan yang lebih selamat serta sejahtera.
Sekian, terima kasih.

"Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?",
dengan peserta menjawab soalan kewangan secara berperingkat untuk menguji pengetahuan dan membuat keputusan di bawah tekanan masa. Program ini dibawakan oleh mySalam dengan sokongan Kementerian Pendidikan Tinggi, serta kerjasama FEN sebagai rakan strategik dan rakan-rakan industri.

Welcoming Remarks by Deputy Governor Dato’ Marzunisham Omar
at the DNFBP Compliance Conference 2026
Sasana Kijang | 22 October 2026
Distinguished guests, representatives of regulatory and supervisory agencies, professional bodies, industry associations, and members of Malaysia's Designated Non-Financial Businesses and Professions (DNFBP).
It is my pleasure to welcome you to the DNFBP Compliance Conference 2026.
This year marks an important milestone in Malaysia's fight against financial crime. Since the enactment of the Anti-Money Laundering Act in 2001. 25 years ago, we have spent a quarter century strengthening our laws, institutions and capabilities against money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing.
Over the 25 years, one lesson becomes increasingly clear. Regulators, law enforcement agencies and financial institutions cannot fight financial crime alone.
Long before illicit funds reach financial system, a company may be incorporated. A transaction may be structured. A legal arrangement may be created. A professional service may be sought.
Each of these moments, someone is standing at the gate
.
Malaysia therefore needs the judgement, diligence and professionalism of all those who help shape our corporate and legal landscape. This is why your presence today matters.
Ladies and gentlemen,
Companies, trusts and legal arrangements, are essential to the economy. But they can be misused to disguise beneficial ownership, conceal origins of illegal proceeds or create a veneer of legitimacy around criminal activity. This places professional service providers, all of you in this room, in a critical position within our fight against financial crime.
The recent conclusion of Malaysia's Mutual Evaluation reaffirmed the importance of this role. DNFBPs are not merely participants in the AML/CFT/CPF framework. You are well placed to detect, prevent and report illicit activities before they enter the financial system.
This responsibility has never been more important. Financial crime is increasingly driven by highly organised criminal networks operating across borders. They leverage on technology, exploit legal structures and continuously adapt their methods. They study our controls and framework. They identify weaknesses and adjust approaches in response to our safeguards. When one avenue is closed, they quickly search for another.
They continuously look for the gate where scrutiny is weakest
.
Across the region, we are seeing sophisticated criminal networks are increasingly exploiting professional services and legitimate business structures to conceal ownership, integrate illicit proceeds and make criminal activities appear legitimate. A recent Transnational Organized Crime Threat Assessment for South-East Asia by UNODC identifies lawyers and accountants among the specialist facilitators within these criminal networks, operating on a contractual basis and providing enabling services to criminal organisations.
Another emerging risk that deserves particular attention is the growing use of corporate mules. Data from the National Fraud Portal points to a rise in corporate mule accounts, reflecting how criminal networks are increasingly exploiting corporate entities to conceal illicit financial flows.
Ladies and gentlemen,
Every ringgit that criminals successfully laundered strengthens criminal enterprises and weakens trust in our institutions. When a professional identifies suspicious activity, refuses to facilitate a questionable arrangement, or submits a suspicious transaction report, that professional is doing far more than meeting a regulatory requirement.
They are closing a gate that criminals were attempting to enter
. In doing so, you are helping to protect businesses, communities and our country.
More than ever, professionals form a vital first line of defence against financial crime. This responsibility goes beyond procedural compliance, it requires professional scepticism, asking critical questions and challenging inconsistencies. And at times, the courage to say "no".
Ultimately, effective gatekeeping depends on sound judgement. It is about understanding who your clients are, where their funds come from, and why certain transactions are being undertaken. The strength of our defences ultimately rests on the quality of those judgements.
As professional services become increasingly digital, these responsibilities become even more critical. Digital onboarding, virtual business relationships and cross-border service delivery have improved efficiency and accessibility. But they also create new opportunities for criminals to conceal identities, misrepresent information and establish seemingly legitimate business relationships. In this environment, our vigilance must evolve alongside technology.
Effective vigilance, however, goes beyond reviewing transactional activity. It requires a deeper understanding of customers, their business activities and the broader context in which they operate. This calls for a risk-based approach. One where professionals recognise behavioural, structural and situational red flags that may indicate potential misuse of their services.
Ladies and gentlemen,
An effective AML/CFT/CPF framework depends not only on strong laws and sound policies, but also on credible supervision and enforcement. This is why Bank Negara Malaysia takes non-compliance seriously. Weaknesses in one part of the system can compromise the integrity of Malaysia's entire AML/CFT framework.
Recent joint enforcement actions involving regulatory and law enforcement agencies reinforce this point. Bank Negara Malaysia and the Companies Commission of Malaysia recently took enforcement action against a company secretary for failing to submit suspicious transaction reports relating to foreign nationals suspected to be involved in an international scam syndicate.
A Labuan investment bank was subjected to enforcement action by Bank Negara Malaysia and the Labuan Financial Services Authority following material deficiencies in customer due diligence that affect the firm’s ability to assess customer’s potential involvement in illicit overseas activities and delays in the submission of suspicious transaction reports.
These cases may involve different sectors and circumstances, but they convey the same message: Weak due diligence, vigilance and reporting create space for criminals to operate. Professional services must never become the gate through which illicit funds acquire the appearance of legitimacy, whether knowingly or unknowingly.
Compliance must therefore be viewed not simply as a regulatory obligation. It is a professional responsibility. Indeed, I would go one step further. AML/CFT compliance is part of the broader duty to uphold the trust placed in every profession represented here.
With that trust comes responsibility. Every client you accept, every company you incorporate, every transaction you review, and every suspicious activity you report is an opportunity to protect the integrity of the system. Individually, these may appear to be routine decisions. But collectively they shape the integrity of Malaysia’s financial and corporate system.
Ladies and gentlemen,
The fight against financial crime ultimately depends on cooperation. No regulator, law enforcement agency or professional service provider can succeed alone. Our defences are strongest when our different perspectives are connected. Only through strong partnerships, meaningful information sharing and collective vigilance can we effectively respond to increasingly sophisticated financial crime threats.
This collaboration will become even more important as we move forward. In 2027, Bank Negara Malaysia will undertake the next iteration National Risk Assessment, which will enable a deeper assessment of the money laundering and terrorism financing risks facing the DNFBP sectors. The findings will support the development of more targeted policies, guidance, and mitigation measures tailored to the specific risks faced by each sector. Your practical insights will be essential. They will help ensure that our policy responses remain effective, proportionate and grounded in the realities faced by each sector.
I would also like to express our sincere appreciation to relevant regulatory agencies, professional bodies and industry associations for their continued cooperation and support. In particular, we thank the Companies Commission of Malaysia, the Malaysian Bar Council, the Malaysian Institute of Accountants, as well as the various industry associations represented here today.
Your work in promoting awareness, facilitating outreach and supporting capacity building has strengthened the resilience of the sector and the community. Let us now build on that partnership, not only by sharing information after risks materialise, but by identifying vulnerabilities earlier and managing them together.
Let me conclude.
Criminals will continue to evolve. They will become faster, more organised and more sophisticated. I have no doubt they will test our controls, exploit complexity and search for the weak points.
But there is one thing they cannot easily overcome: A community of professionals committed to integrity. They cannot overcome professionals who ask critical questions. They cannot overcome a culture where suspicious activities are questioned rather than ignored. And they cannot overcome institutions that share information and act with a common purpose.
In short, they cannot overcome a system in which every gate is guarded with sound good judgement, vigilance and courage
.
Let us leave this conference with a renewed sense of purpose, a stronger commitment to vigilance, and a shared determination to protect the integrity of Malaysia's financial and corporate system.
Each of us stands at a different gate
. But all of us protect the same system. Together, let us keep that system worthy of the trust Malaysia places in it.
Terima kasih and I wish you a productive conference.
Bank Negara Malaysia
22 October 2026
title: Deputy Governor's Welcoming Remarks at the DNFBP Compliance Conference 2026

Special Address by Governor Dato’ Sri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour
at the 21st Kuala Lumpur Islamic Finance Forum (KLIFF) 2026
Kuala Lumpur | 20 October 2026
'Islamic Finance for Impact – The Next Measure of Success'
It is a pleasure to be here at the 21st Kuala Lumpur Islamic Finance Forum.
From scale to impact
Over the last five decades, Islamic finance has demonstrated its capacity to grow. Our first steps were to build credibility, strong foundations, and scale. At the midpoint, the focus shifted towards strengthening competitiveness, innovation, and capabilities.
Today, the context is markedly different. Economies are confronting climate risks, demographic change, wider developmental needs and geopolitical fragmentation. These forces are reshaping our economies and financing needs.
This year’s theme for KLIFF speaks directly to this task. It invites us to look beyond scale and consider outcomes. It raises the standard by which Islamic finance should now be measured. The challenge is to demonstrate not only continued strength, but greater relevance to the economies and societies it serves.
The question before us today can no longer simply be: “Can Islamic finance compete and grow?”. Rather, we must ask a more consequential question:
'What does that growth now enable?'
'What opportunities can it create?'
'What outcomes can it deliver?'
At the recent Financial Institutions Directors' Education (FIDE) programme, I asked whether we are still financing yesterday's economy or positioning ourselves for Malaysia’s next phase of growth. Today, I want to take that conversation one step further. Not just what Islamic finance should finance. But what that should achieve and how do we measure our success.
Redefining the measure of success
This focus on outcomes is not new. It is rooted in the foundations of Islamic finance. History reminds us that finance was not understood as an end in itself, but as a means of supporting broader economic and societal objectives. The legitimacy of financial activity was closely connected to the value it created beyond individual transactions.
Consider the great
külliye
complexes of the Ottoman Empire
[1]
– including the remarkable Süleymaniye Complex. Sustained through
waqf
,
they brought together schools, hospitals, libraries, welfare services, and commerce.
They were not just a collection of buildings. They were a complete ecosystem built around a mosque, designed to create lasting societal outcomes. Success was measured by the greater purpose it sought:
to improve education;
to enhance health services;
to enable more upward social mobility; and
to strengthen community wellbeing across generations.
There is an important lesson here: The resources mattered, but the outcomes mattered more.
This calls for us to widen our measure of success:
From assets to outcomes;
From transactions to transformation;
From financial inclusion to meaningful economic participation;
From Shariah compliance to the fulfilment of Shariah purpose; and
From growth of finance to growth enabled by finance.
These measures represent an evolution in how we understand role of finance and its contributions to society and economy.
Finance that empowers
This perspective is especially relevant in the context of financial inclusion and economic participation, where financial access itself should not be viewed as the final and desired outcome. This matters in Malaysia, where Micro, Small and Medium enterprises (MSMEs) contributed almost 40% of GDP
[2]
and accounted for almost 50% of total employment in 2025 – with more than three-quarters of them are microenterprises. Yet, many of these businesses continue to face challenges beyond access to finance.
Today, Malaysia’s social finance initiative, iTEKAD
[3]
offers a practical illustration. At first glance, it is a social finance programme. But financing alone does not create empowerment. Sustainable, lasting empowerment requires:
financing and protection,
financing and capability,
financing and access to markets.
Put together, these elements help microentrepreneurs build stronger and more sustainable livelihoods. It addresses the interconnected constraints that can prevent low-income entrepreneurs from sustaining and expanding their businesses.
iTEKAD has supported nearly sixteen thousand participants through its entrepreneurship, employment, and protection programmes. But its impact is best understood through the lives it transformed. Let me share the story of Puan Fauziah, a microentrepreneur from Klang.
Puan Fauziah began with a home-based business selling traditional ginger floss for postpartum mothers. Like many, she had determination. What she lacked were the resources to grow. Through iTEKAD’s grant financing and entrepreneurship training, her business expanded. Today, she reaches customers through digital platforms and has even exported to the United Kingdom through a halal marketplace.
That is the outcome that matters. A stronger livelihood, greater resilience and upward economic mobility.
This also brings us to an equally important consideration on capital allocation. Capital is never passive. Every financing decision shapes the economy. It influences which sectors expand, which businesses grow and which innovations receive support. Capital allocation is therefore an act of stewardship of the nation’s economy.
Strengthening Malaysia’s productive capacity requires capital to flow to the right places. Traditional approaches may no longer be sufficient. Islamic finance can provide innovative risk-sharing solutions, especially where broader capital sources, structures and different risk profiles are needed. Through i-CITA, launched in 2025, Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) is facilitating industry learning in offering risk-sharing solutions for key areas such as food security and climate resilience.
Collective stewardship, greater impact
These challenges cannot be addressed through isolated efforts. Impact must be a shared endeavour. Regulators, financial institutions, Shariah scholars, and the wider industry must work together to build the ecosystem that impactful innovation requires.
At BNM, our role is to enable innovation, support responsible risk-taking and create a conducive environment for impactful solutions. The Digital Asset Innovation Hub launched in June 2025 provides one platform for the industry to explore emerging technologies and use cases with real economic value.
We are also reviewing the Shariah Contract Framework to promote broader and more effective application of Shariah contracts. We will be issuing a Strategy Paper and Exposure Draft this year.
The next Financial Sector Blueprint will also carry this broader shift. We want to align the financial sector more closely with Malaysia's future socioeconomic priorities. Our measure of success must also evolve in tandem.
As we look ahead, three priorities warrant our focus:
First, align strategies and capital
with purpose.
This means directing resources towards higher-value sectors and renewable energy and strengthening resilience against climate and economic shocks.
Second,
innovate around real needs.
We want to build on existing efforts to design solutions around the realities faced by households, and businesses, particularly where needs remain underserved or unmet. This includes financial and technical support for the expansion of halal MSMEs.
Third, keep values at the centre.
Fairness, integrity, empathy. These values must remain central to business decisions and market conduct.
Maqasid Shariah
is our compass. We want to get to impactful value-based outcomes.
Islamic finance has travelled far.
It has built scale.
It has built sophistication.
It has built credibility.
Now, the next measure of success is where we go from here.
A more productive economy.
More resilient communities.
More widely shared opportunities.
Scale tells us how far we have travelled. Purpose must remain as our true north to a better future.
That, in my view, is the next measure of success for Islamic finance.
Bank Negara Malaysia
20 October 2026
[1]
Avcıoğlu, N. (2024). The Külliye as hypotext: A new reading of Ottoman imperial mosques and tombs. Journal of Material Cultures in the Muslim World, 4(2), 230–251
[2]
Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM), Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) Performance 2025.
[3]
iTEKAD Entrepreneurship was launched in 2020, iTEKAD Protection in 2025, while iTEKAD Employment was launched in July 2026.

Opening Address by Assistant Governor Mohamad Ali Iqbal
at IFMC Roundtable 2026
Kuala Lumpur | 19 October 2026
It is my great pleasure to be part of this Islamic Financial Market Committee Roundtable 2026. I welcome all of you to this gathering that offers an excellent platform to deepen our discussions while strengthening our collaboration and trust within the Islamic financial market community.
Introduction: Islamic Finance Milestones
Ladies and gentlemen,
Malaysia has built a strong foundation in Islamic finance, reflected in its ranking in the Islamic Finance Development Indicator (IFDI)
[1]
for 13 consecutive years, and Malaysia accounts for approximately 36% of global sukuk outstanding.
Domestically, Islamic finance has become an integral part of the financial system. Islamic financing now represents almost half of total financing within the banking sector, while the Islamic capital market represents about two-third of the capital market. At the same time, the Islamic financial market has attained depth and sophistication, with transactions in Malaysia’s unsecured Islamic interbank market exceeding RM1 trillion in 2025, more than twice the level recorded five years ago. Moreover, as at 30 September 2026, cumulative unsecured Islamic interbank transactions reached RM1.27 trillion, exceeding the RM1.19 trillion recorded in the conventional market, reflecting the depth and relative strength of the Islamic money market.
These advancements are a testament to the long-standing commitment of many stakeholders across the ecosystem, including the ones here. They reflect decades of sustained investment in market infrastructure, regulatory and Shariah frameworks, institutional capabilities, talent development and strong industry collaboration.
Building Tomorrow’s Islamic Financial market – Three shifts for the next chapter
Ladies and gentlemen,
While these achievements provide much to be proud of, they are not the destination. Rather, they provide the foundation upon which the next phase of development must be built.
The more important question today is not how far the market has come, but whether it is equipped for what comes next. As we look ahead, I believe the next chapter of Malaysia's Islamic financial market will be defined by three important shifts.
The first shift;
from market size to deeper and broader market participation.
Malaysia has built a sizeable and increasingly liquid Islamic financial market. The Malaysian Government Investment Issue (MGII) has grown in prominence over the years and is now broadly comparable to the conventional Malaysian Government Securities (MGS) in both size and liquidity. Outstanding MGII now stood at RM640 billion, representing 47% of total outstanding government securities. Secondary market activity has also expanded significantly.
Nevertheless, there remains substantial opportunity to further deepen the market by broadening participation across a wider spectrum of investors. For instance, foreign holdings of MGII remain relatively modest at only around 8%, compared to 34% for MGS. This suggests an untapped potential to attract a broader pool of international investors into Malaysia's sukuk market. Encouragingly, the signals from global investors remain strong. Malaysia's USD1.5 billion Global Sukuk issuance in July 2026 attracted more than USD9.5 billion in orders and achieved an oversubscription rate of 4.7 times, and more importantly, at record-low spreads of 15 basis points above comparable US Treasury yields for the 5.75-year tranche and 25 basis points for the 10-year tranche. Indeed, market pricing was observed to be 'priced like a AA-rated country', underscoring strong global confidence in Malaysia's economic fundamentals and prospects.
Broadening the investor base across segments requires a market that investors can readily understand, access, price and trade with confidence. It calls for greater transparency, internationally recognised sukuk structures and deeper secondary market liquidity that supports efficient price discovery and trading activity. Recent engagements with Japanese investors, led by the IFMC, revealed growing interest in Malaysia's sukuk market, demonstrating that the foundations are in place to attract participation from international investors.
The second shift; from innovative landmark transactions to scalable market solutions
. Malaysia's Islamic financial market has long been recognised for its ability to innovate and pioneer new developments. In recent years, we have witnessed several important milestones that demonstrate both the dynamism of the market and its willingness to embrace new possibilities.
These include Malaysia's first tokenised sukuk, which showcased the potential of distributed ledger technology to enhance market efficiency and accessibility. We also saw Malaysia's first pilot involving the settlement of tokenised sukuk using tokenised deposits.
The market has also continued to advance solutions that deliver meaningful societal impact. The world's first blue sukuk, for example, channelled proceeds towards critical domestic water infrastructure projects, supporting sustainable water resource management and strengthening water security for communities.
These developments signal an important shift from conceptual exploration towards practical implementation, where new ideas are applied to address real market needs and deliver tangible economic and social outcomes. They also reflect the strength of collaboration across the ecosystem, bringing together regulators, financial institutions, market infrastructures and other stakeholders to turn innovative concepts into reality. These are significant achievements and milestones worth celebrating. I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate those who have played a role in driving these initiatives forward and contributing to the continued development of Malaysia's Islamic financial market.
Looking ahead, there remains significant opportunity to build on this strong momentum. As new ideas continue to emerge, our collective next task is to ensure that successful innovations achieve broader adoption and create lasting impact across the market. The first transaction proves possibility, the next requires scale.
We therefore encourage the continued development of innovative Shariah-compliant solutions that address genuine economic needs, create value and importantly, achieve scale. The real impact of these innovations will ultimately depend on their broader adoption, repeat transactions and deeper market participation.
Third shift; from market benchmark to market integrity.
A deep and resilient Islamic financial market rests on a foundation of strong market integrity. The strength of a market is determined not only by the products it offers or the transactions it facilitates, but also by the confidence it inspires among market participants. This confidence is reflected in how instruments are priced, how risks are managed, and how market participants value, transact and make decisions across the financial system.
One important initiative in this regard is the introduction of MYOR-i, the world's first transaction-based Islamic benchmark rate. This represents a significant milestone in the development of Malaysia's Islamic financial market. By anchoring pricing to actual Islamic money market transactions, the benchmark rate strengthens transparency and supports greater confidence in the pricing and valuation of Islamic financial instruments.
Recent developments have been encouraging. The issuance of Malaysia's first MYOR-i-referenced sukuk and MYOR-i-referenced Islamic profit rate swap represent important steps forward. These developments demonstrate that market participants are increasingly prepared to incorporate the benchmark into their business activities and inspire further confidence that the transition is gaining momentum across the market.
Importantly, the transition to MYOR-i forms part of broader efforts to further strengthen the integrity and resilience of Malaysia's Islamic financial market. These efforts include enhancing market liquidity, supporting effective market-making activities, strengthening risk management capabilities and fostering a more active secondary market.
The next phase is about achieving broader adoption across financing, sukuk and derivatives instruments. This will require coordinated action across the industry, including system enhancements, product development, documentation readiness, robust fallback arrangements, and wider adoption of the Tahawwut Master Agreement. Success will depend not only on individual institutional readiness, but also on collective commitment across the market ecosystem.
This year's IFMC Roundtable therefore takes place at a particularly important juncture. The industry is moving towards market-wide adoption and readiness ahead of the mandatory transition on 1 July 2027 – yet we know that the success of MYOR-i will not ultimately be measured by the date on which its use becomes mandatory.
Rather, it will be measured by the confidence with which market participants price instruments, execute transactions, hedge risks and manage liquidity using the benchmark in their daily business activities. Because in the end, confidence is at the heart of every well-functioning financial market. And such confidence, underpinned by robust, transparent and credible market benchmarks, is essential to preserving the integrity of Malaysia's Islamic financial market.
Call to action: From Milestones to Market Practice
Ladies and gentlemen,
Malaysia's recent milestones demonstrated that we know how to pioneer innovation. From advancing innovative and sustainable finance solutions, the industry has consistently shown its ability to lead and innovate. These achievements provide a strong foundation for the next phase of development. The opportunity before us now is to move beyond individual success stories and transform promising milestones into common market practices, embedded in the day-to-day activities of issuers, investors, intermediaries and end-users.
After all, markets do not deepen through isolated transactions. Markets deepen when more participants are willing to issue, invest, trade, hedge and provide liquidity. Market developed ultimately through repeated use, growing confidence and widespread participation.
Conclusion
The discussion we have today therefore matters. The decisions we make, the partnerships we forge, and the actions we take collectively will help shape the trajectory of Malaysia's Islamic financial market for decades to come. This is a journey that requires not only vision, but also collaboration and collective commitment.
In this regard, let us be guided by the timeless wisdom of the Qur'an:
'
Cooperate with one another in goodness and righteousness, and do not cooperate in sin and transgression
.
'
(Surah Al-Ma'idah, Verse 2)
May this divine command for cooperation continue to guide our efforts as we work together to strengthen Malaysia's Islamic financial market and advance its contribution to sustainable economic and financial development that is blessed by the Almighty. On this note, let the IFMC Roundtable Discussions begin – I wish you all a productive discourse ahead. Thank you.
[1]
By ICD-LSEG Islamic Finance Development Reports

Opening Remarks by Deputy Governor Adnan Zaylani Mohamad Zahid
at the 11th ASEAN Central Bank Heads of Internal Audit Network Meeting
Kuala Lumpur | 8 October 2026
A very warm welcome to Kuala Lumpur and to Bank Negara Malaysia. It is a pleasure to join you at the 11th ASEAN Central Bank Heads of Internal Audit Network Meeting. Your presence reflects our shared commitment to advancing the internal audit profession and strengthening the institutions we serve.
This year's gathering is special as, for the first time, we welcome representatives from Papua New Guinea. This reflects the growing spirit of regional cooperation among our audit communities. Over the years, our Network has evolved beyond a professional forum into a trusted platform for exchanging perspectives and learning from one another's experience.
Such collaboration is increasingly important. We operate in an environment transformed by technological advances, increasingly sophisticated cyber threats, geopolitical developments, economic uncertainty, and demanding stakeholder expectations. Risks are becoming more interconnected, and events in one institution, sector or jurisdiction can quickly have wider implications.
At their core, central banks are institutions of trust. Whether pursuing price stability, safeguarding financial stability, ensuring the smooth functioning of payment and settlement systems, managing reserves, or supporting economic resilience, our effectiveness depends on confidence in our institutions. Without that confidence, even well-designed policies and robust frameworks may not be effective. Preserving trust must therefore be one of our most important responsibilities.
Let me share
five
areas of risks that are top of mind when it comes to preserving trust and confidence, relevant for our discussions.
First
, its cross-border nature. Cyberattacks now transcend national borders, while artificial intelligence has implications across jurisdictions. Digital assets and interconnected financial ecosystems create risks and dependencies that may not be fully understood in isolation. By bringing together diverse perspectives and practical experiences, we can strengthen our collective capacity to identify emerging risks and develop more effective responses.
Second
, uncertainty is no longer episodic. It is more prevalent. Important decisions have to be made, more often, with incomplete information and in rapidly changing circumstances. Our challenge is therefore not to eliminate uncertainty, but to strengthen our capacity to navigate it responsibly and confidently.
Third
, data increasingly underpins critical decisions across policymaking, supervision, financial market operations and organisational management. Confidence in those decisions depends on confidence in the underlying data, making sound data governance essential to institutional credibility.
Fourth
, artificial intelligence presents both opportunity and responsibility. It can strengthen analysis, improve efficiency, enhance risk sensing, and augment human decision-making, but it also raises questions about accountability, transparency, data quality and ethical use. The question now is beyond whether to adopt these technologies, but how to use and govern them responsibly, with clear accountability, meaningful human oversight and explainable decisions consistent with our values.
And finally,
resilience has become a strategic imperative. A central bank's capacity to fulfil its mandate must endure through cyber incidents, operational disruptions, and market stress. Resilience is demonstrated not by the absence of disruption, but by the ability to anticipate, withstand, recover from, and adapt to it while continuing to deliver critical functions and sustain public confidence.
Against this backdrop, the role of internal audit is evolving. Its traditional responsibility to provide independent assurance on controls, governance, and compliance remains fundamental. However, boards and senior management increasingly expect insights that help institutions prepare for future challenges, identify emerging vulnerabilities and assess readiness for what lies ahead. Internal audit is therefore operating more visibly at the intersection of governance, risk, technology, and strategy.
This evolution brings considerable expectations. When a risk materialises, one of the first questions often asked is, 'Where was internal audit?' The question reflects confidence in the function, but no assurance provider can anticipate every future event, examine every risk, or guarantee every outcome. The appropriate response is neither to retreat from accountability nor to offer assurances that may not be reasonably fulfilled, but to establish a shared and disciplined understanding of what effective assurance can deliver.
The true value of internal audit lies in improving the quality of institutional judgement. This requires clarity on the most significant risks, disciplined prioritisation, and open dialogue among internal audit, boards and management on the nature, scope, and limitations of assurance.
Looking ahead, the most effective internal audit functions will combine technological capability with sound professional judgement. They will be agile in responding to emerging risks, courageous in challenging established assumptions, and strategic in understanding the broader environment in which their institutions operate.
Most importantly, they will remain trusted by upholding qualities that cannot be automated: independence, impartiality, professional scepticism, and integrity. Technology can extend reach, sharpen analysis and improve timeliness, but it cannot replace the judgement, courage, and ethical grounding that give assurance its credibility.
This year's theme,
'Reimagining Assurance: Harnessing Intelligence, Resilience and Integrity'
, speaks directly to this evolution. It is about transforming data into insight and foresight, assessing whether institutions can operate effectively through disruption and change, and preserving the integrity essential to every central bank's credibility. Reimagining assurance therefore extends beyond new tools or methodologies. It requires the profession to remain relevant and responsive in an increasingly complex world.
These themes are reflected throughout the programme, including auditing artificial intelligence, emerging cyber threats and recovery, cybersecurity readiness, data management, and the Global Internal Audit Standards. Though diverse, these topics share a common objective: enabling internal audit to remain relevant, rigorous, and responsive to the changing needs of central banks.
I encourage everyone to engage openly, sharing your successes, and also lessons from challenges and setbacks. Throughout today’s discussions, let us draw on our respective experiences, challenge established thinking, and consider how assurance can continue to evolve in support of stronger and more resilient central banks.
I am confident that this meeting will generate meaningful insights, deepen regional collaboration, and further strengthen the ASEAN central banks' internal audit community. With that, it gives me great pleasure to officially declare the commencement of the 11th ASEAN Central Bank Heads of Internal Audit Network Meeting.

Special Address by Governor Dato’ Sri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour
at the 16th International Conference
on Financial Crime and Counter Terrorism Financing (IFCTF) 2026
Kuala Lumpur | 6 October 2026
'Intelligence-Led Financial Crime Prevention: The Power of Data, Insights and Collaboration'
Let me begin by congratulating AICB, the Compliance Officer Networking Group and everyone involved in organising today’s conference.
This year marks an important milestone in our fight against financial crime. It has been 25 years since Malaysia enacted the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing, Anti-Restricted Activity Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001 (AMLA).
Over the past quarter century, we have transformed what began as a traditional AML framework into a comprehensive regime that combats all forms of financial crimes. This progress has been built on three foundations:
First, stronger laws. This includes several rounds of AMLA amendments and enhancements to other key legislations. Together, these measures enhanced our ability to investigate, prosecute and recover illicit assets. They also strengthened transparency, reinforced accountability.
Second, stronger institutions, anchored by a whole-of-nation approach. Over the years, Malaysia has established key platforms for coordination and intelligence sharing - including the National Anti-Financial Crime Centre (NFCC), National Scam Response Center (NSRC), Multi-Agency Task Force (MATF), the National Fraud Portal and MyFINet. Together, they strengthened our collective response to financial crime, reflecting our shared belief that no single institution can tackle these threats alone.
Third, stronger understanding of risk and supervisory approach. Five comprehensive National ML/TF Risk Assessments, complemented by thematic assessments, have sharpened our understanding of threats and vulnerabilities. Regulation and supervision have also made significant progress. Today, with more than 27,000 financial and non-financial reporting institutions, supported by a robust framework and technology-enabled supervision - we are able to deliver effective and risk-appropriate oversight.
Together, these efforts have strengthened Malaysia’s AML/CFT/CPF regime, culminating in the positive recognition in the 2025 Mutual Evaluation.
More importantly, they have delivered tangible results. For example, in the first half of 2026 alone, the financial sector has prevented approximately RM1.9 billion in attempted fraudulent transactions, surpassing the RM1.2 billion prevented during the whole of 2025
[1]
. More than RM37 billion of assets have also been recovered in the past five years
[2]
. Prominent and complex financial crime cases were also investigated and prosecuted, including those involving multiple agencies.
These achievements are a testament to our whole-of-nation efforts. I express my deepest appreciation to all agencies, institutions and individuals who have contributed to this journey. Well done everyone.
Ladies and gentlemen,
Earlier this year, at the Sasana Symposium at Bank Negara Malaysia, I spoke about the Gelam tree. Some of you who were there will recall this. The Gelam tree, which grows along the East coast, thrives in harsh conditions because it continually sheds its bark, keeping itself in a constant state of renewal.
Over the past quarter century, we have strengthened the laws, institutions and partnerships. Yet the work is never complete. As criminals adapt, technologies evolve and risks become more complex, so too must our response.
Like the Gelam tree, our resilience will depend not on what we have achieved, but on our ability to continually renew and prepare ourselves for the challenges ahead.
Two forces, in particular, demand our attention.
First, financial crime is not immune to global fragmentation and uncertainties.
Geopolitical developments are reshaping the movement of money, goods and information. New payment channels, more seamless cross-border flows and evolving trade corridors create fertile grounds for illicit activities. As international cooperation becomes more complex and under greater strain, blind spots may emerge.
Thus, as emphasized by the FATF international standards, geopolitical developments should be incorporated into risk assessments and risk-based approaches. We must continuously reassess our exposures, strengthen existing measures, and remain vigilant in navigating the shifting currents.
Secondly, driven by technology, financial crime is moving from fast to faster.
Technology has transformed how we access financial services, transact, and connect. Unfortunately, it is also changing how criminals finance and disguise their activities. Criminals no longer operate at the speed of people. They operate at the speed of technology.
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a case in point. AI-generated content can now mimick voices and appearances with remarkable realism, making fraud increasingly difficult to detect. I am sure many of you have seen the deepfake video of me arguing with a guest on live TV. With AI, it is easier for criminals to socially engineer and manipulate victims. Today, about 95% of online fraud cases involve victims who are deceived into transferring funds themselves.
AI Agents can power fraud campaigns, identify vulnerabilities and amplify cyberattacks. INTERPOL estimates AI-enabled fraud to be 4.5 times more profitable than traditional methods
[3]
, enabling criminals to operate faster, reach further and inflict greater harm.
These developments put us in an 'Arms Race' against criminals. So, as they automate deception, we must automate detection. As they exploit speed and scale, we must become more agile to identify, disrupt, and prevent illicit activities.
Ladies and gentlemen,
The conference theme today – '
Intelligence-Led Financial Crime Prevention: The Power of Data, Insights and Collaboration',
points us towards the future.
Let’s start with the Power of Data and Insights.
In today’s digital economy, every transaction leaves a trail of data. The challenge is no longer the availability of information, but our ability to transform them into actionable insights and intelligence.
At Bank Negara Malaysia, as the Financial Intelligence Unit of the country, data and insights are at the core of our work. From generating intelligence products, to facilitating data management, we continuously strengthen our processes and infrastructure that supports data-led intelligence.
Yet, there is more to be done. Around the world, technology and advanced analytics are being leveraged to strengthen fraud prevention. Malaysia is no exception. Since October 2025, the National Fraud Portal has piloted the analysis of payment network patterns to identify potential mule accounts. To date, PayNet has flagged more than 1,600 suspicious accounts, many of which were subsequently assessed as presenting mule-related risks. This demonstrates the potential of network-level intelligence, by connecting information across financial institutions, to identify risks that may appear invisible from the perspective of any one individual institution.
To support this shift, BNM has strengthened the foundations for technology risk management and fraud prevention. The revised
Risk Management in Technology
policy document strengthens financial institutions’ resilience against technology-related risks, cyber risks and rapidly evolving digital crimes. Meanwhile, the recently issued
Financial Institutions' Response to Fraud
policy document further reinforces accountability for fraud risk management while promoting the responsible use of intelligence, analytics and technologies.
This is only the beginning. Building on these foundations, the banking industry and PayNet are working towards introducing industry-wide fraud alert capabilities that can warn banks and customers of potential risks before a transaction is completed. These alerts will prompt customers to pause, think and verify before proceeding. We recognise that this capability may introduce additional friction for customers. However, these measures are necessary to strike an appropriate balance between offering convenience and protecting customers from fraud, particularly authorised scams. Today, I am pleased to announce that a pilot testing involving selected banks is targeted for first half of 2027, ahead of wider implementation.
Ladies and gentlemen,
The future of fraud management cannot be built on detecting suspicious activity after the fact. We need to move from a reactive model to a predictive one, and ultimately to a preventive one. The greatest success is the fraud that never happens.
As today’s theme suggests, no problem of this scale can be solved alone.
For 25-years, AMLA has supported a whole-of-nation approach, bringing together the public and private sector stakeholders together to combat financial crime. Building on Malaysia’s strength in domestic coordination, there are two areas where we can do even more.
The first is on information sharing. While public-private partnerships have delivered tangible results, there remains significant untapped potential in industry-led collaboration and private-private partnership. From the development of sector-driven guidance, to establishing shared infrastructure, stronger private sector cooperation can substantially enhance our ability to respond to emerging risks. Looking ahead, we should also move from ad-hoc information exchanges towards a more structured, transnational and technology-enabled partnerships. Underpinned by trust, sound governance structure, and secure information-sharing mechanisms, the potential of both public-private and private-private partnerships can be powerful enablers to advance intelligence-led financial crime prevention.
The second area is on international cooperation. From informal cooperation through the exchange of intelligence, to formal cooperation for investigation and prosecution, international cooperation is essential to building a complete picture of financial crime risks. Criminal networks know no borders, therefore we cannot be limited by national boundaries.
Ladies and gentlemen,
As we look ahead, allow me to leave you with four simple reminders drawn from the very Act, AMLA, that has guided us over the past quarter century:
A – Anticipate
emerging threats, because yesterday’s solution will not solve tomorrow’s problems;
M – Monitor
risks diligently, because awareness is the foundation of resilience;
L – Leverage
technology responsibly, because innovation brings both opportunities and risks; and
A – Act together,
because no institution, no sector and no country can confront financial crime alone.
When we look back on the next 25 years, I hope that we will not simply count the laws amended, policies introduced, or standards met. Rather, I hope we will be able to say:
That we protected people from harm.
That we safeguarded the integrity of our financial system.
And that we left behind a stronger, safer and more resilient Malaysia than the one we inherited.
Because ultimately, the true measure of our success is not the compliance we achieve.
It is the trust we preserve.
The best chapters of Malaysia's AML/CFT/CPF journey are still ahead of us.
Let us write and shape them together.
[1]
Source: Bank Negara Malaysia

Mutual Evaluation of Malaysia
(December 2025)
[3]
INTERPOL report warns of increasingly sophisticated global financial fraud threat
(March 2026)
